Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.

revision_notes: Light fast-path search surfaced an ITU-attributed figure, so the row was escalated to the full path rather than confirmed as Unknown. ITU data reproduced by TheGlobalEconomy.com show international bandwidth per internet user at just 0.27 kbit/s in 2016 (declining from 5.51 kbit/s in 2012, the last year ITU data are shown for this country), which would score code 1 (Very Low, <5 kbit/s). However, the World Bank's Digital Development Site (mAccess Diagnostic Tool, accessed 2023) cites a materially different estimate of 14.26 kbit/s per user, which would score code 2 (Low, 5-19 kbit/s). ITU's Facts and Figures 2023 report shows the LDC average bandwidth usage reached 37.7 kbit/s per user by 2022, suggesting Madagascar's true current figure is likely well above the stale 2016 ITU value, but the two country-specific sources found cannot be reconciled with confidence and no clean current ITU country profile could be retrieved (ITU DataHub is JavaScript-rendered and not directly scrapeable). Flagged for human review rather than guessing between codes 1 and 2.
revised_comments: ITU data indicate very low international bandwidth per internet user in Madagascar (0.27 kbit/s in 2016, the most recent country-specific ITU figure located), reflecting the country's historically limited international connectivity; other, less clearly sourced estimates put the more recent figure closer to 14 kbit/s per user, consistent with capacity added through new submarine and terrestrial fibre links serving the region.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
Comments: No data found after thorough searching
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light fast-path search surfaced JIRAMA tariff data and World Bank income data, so the row was escalated to full verification. Madagascar's average residential electricity tariff is approximately USD 0.12-0.14/kWh (2022-2025, JIRAMA via globalpetrolprices.com and nyongesasande.com), against a GNI per capita of only USD 510 (2024, World Bank). Applying the World Bank/ESMAP standard affordability benchmark (cost of a 30 kWh/month subsistence consumption as a share of monthly income), the bill represents roughly 9-10% of monthly GNI per capita, placing Madagascar on the boundary between 'Expensive (6-10%)' (code 2) and 'Very Expensive (>10%)' (code 1); using a more realistic average household consumption of around 50 kWh/month, the share rises to over 15%, implying code 1. The World Bank's 'Falling Short' tariff-design study (2020) and an earlier ESMAP/AFREA subsidy study both explicitly name Madagascar among the countries with the most severe electricity affordability problems in the developing world, driven by very low per-capita income rather than an exceptionally high tariff. Given the sensitivity of the resulting code to the consumption assumption used, this is flagged for human review rather than asserting a single value.
revised_comments: Madagascar's residential electricity tariff has averaged around USD 0.12-0.14 per kWh in recent years (JIRAMA, 2022-2025), a cost that consumes a large share of typical household income given a GNI per capita of only around USD 510 (2024). The World Bank identifies Madagascar as one of the countries with the most acute electricity affordability challenges in Sub-Saharan Africa, a problem driven primarily by very low per-capita incomes rather than by exceptionally high tariffs.
